Because the written word is not inherently more or less serious than spoken words. Communication by text can be just as poignant and meaningful as a face to face conversation. Most people seem to view mockery and insults on the internet just the same as they would view such things delivered to their face.

There's a gap in perception of Internet communications that could be described as generational, though it's not a matter of age necessarily. I've noticed that people who've been around using the internet for well over a decade, the folks whose first major entry to the Internet was probably the AOL home page that popped up after they connected on their dial-up, seem less prone to getting upset about things on the internet. Those whose main entry to the Internet was MySpace or Facebook or similar seem to take things more personally on average. It's by no means universally true, but the trend exists in my experience at least.

Anyway, my armchair psychology assessment is that it's a matter of perception and experience. Those who first experienced the internet as impersonal and anonymous seem to be less likely to take it seriously, and those who first experienced it as an extension of their offline social life seem to treat it with the seriousness of their offline life. There happen to be far more of the latter group, thus those of us who can put a barrier between the internet and our emotions are in the minority.
